26  The Generalized Minimal Residual (GMRES) Method

For a nonsymmetric matrix, the SPD energy argument no longer supplies an objective to minimize. The residual norm remains meaningful: we can choose the available correction that best satisfies the equations. GMRES applies this choice to an expanding Krylov subspace (Saad and Schultz 1986).

Arnoldi provides orthonormal coordinates for the corrections and their images under \(\bA\). In those coordinates, the minimization becomes a small least-squares problem. We derive that reduction, update its solution with plane rotations, and examine what is lost when the stored basis is discarded at a restart.

26.1 Reduction to Hessenberg Least Squares

Let \(\br^{(0)}=\bb-\bA\bx^{(0)}\) be nonzero and let \(\beta=\|\br^{(0)}\|_2\). We run the Arnoldi iteration of the referenced result from \(\bv_1=\br^{(0)}/\beta\). By the referenced result, after \(k\) steps the columns of \(\bV_k\) form an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\br^{(0)})\) and \(\bA\bV_k=\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k\). These two facts reduce the residual minimization in \(\fR^n\) to a small least-squares problem.

At the first step, the correction has the form \(\alpha\br^{(0)}\). We therefore minimize \(\|\br^{(0)}-\alpha\bA\br^{(0)}\|_2\). The next exercise solves this scalar problem. Later steps allow more correction directions, but apply the same least-squares principle.

WarningExercise

Assume \(\bA\br^{(0)}\neq\bzero\). Expand the squared residual and derive \[ \begin{align} \alpha=\frac{(\bA\br^{(0)})^T\br^{(0)}}{\|\bA\br^{(0)}\|_2^2}. \end{align} \] Compare this with the first CG step for an SPD matrix. Which quantity is each method minimizing? Find an invertible matrix and a nonzero residual for which this first GMRES correction is zero.

NoteTheorem: The GMRES Projected Least-Squares Problem

Assume the Arnoldi process has completed \(k\) steps without breakdown. Let any vector in the affine space \(\bx^{(0)} + \mathcal{K}_k(\bA, \br^{(0)})\) be parameterized as \(\bx = \bx^{(0)} + \bV_k \by\) for some vector \(\by \in \fR^k\). The residual vector satisfies \[ \begin{align} \br(\bx) = \bb - \bA(\bx^{(0)} + \bV_k \by) = \br^{(0)} - \bA \bV_k \by = \beta \bv_1 - \bV_{k+1} \bar{\bH}_k \by = \bV_{k+1} (\beta \be_1 - \bar{\bH}_k \by). \end{align} \] Because the columns of \(\bV_{k+1}\) are orthonormal, \(\bV_{k+1}\) is an isometry in the Euclidean norm: \[ \begin{align} \|\bb - \bA\bx\|_2 = \|\beta \be_1 - \bar{\bH}_k \by\|_2, \end{align} \] where \(\be_1 = (1, 0, ..., 0)^T \in \fR^{k+1}\). The GMRES iterate is \(\bx^{(k)} = \bx^{(0)} + \bV_k \by_k\), where \(\by_k\) uniquely solves the \((k+1) \times k\) upper Hessenberg least-squares problem \[ \begin{align} \by_k = \arg\min_{\by \in \fR^k} \|\beta \be_1 - \bar{\bH}_k \by\|_2. \end{align} \]

TipProof

The unknown in the reduced problem is the coefficient vector \(\by\), not the full vector \(\bx\). Since \(\bV_k\) is a basis of the correction space, every admissible approximation has a unique representation \(\bx=\bx^{(0)}+\bV_k\by\).

Substitute it into the residual and keep track of the dimensions. The Arnoldi relation uses \(\bar{\bH}_k\in\fR^{(k+1)\times k}\) and \(\bV_{k+1}\in\fR^{n\times(k+1)}\): \[ \begin{align} \bb-\bA\bx &=\bb-\bA\bx^{(0)}-\bA\bV_k\by\\ &=\br^{(0)}-\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k\by\\ &=\beta\bv_1-\bV_{k+1}\bar{\bH}_k\by\\ &=\bV_{k+1}(\beta\be_1-\bar{\bH}_k\by). \end{align} \] The last equality uses \(\bV_{k+1}\be_1=\bv_1\).

Put \(\bz=\beta\be_1-\bar{\bH}_k\by\). Orthonormality gives \[ \begin{align} \|\bV_{k+1}\bz\|_2^2 =\bz^T\bV_{k+1}^T\bV_{k+1}\bz =\bz^T\bz=\|\bz\|_2^2. \end{align} \] Taking square roots proves equality of the full and reduced residual norms for every coefficient vector. Hence minimizing one is exactly equivalent to minimizing the other.

For uniqueness, suppose \(\bar{\bH}_k\by=\bzero\). Its last row gives \(h_{k+1,k}y_k=0\). Before breakdown this subdiagonal entry is nonzero, so \(y_k=0\). The preceding row then gives \(h_{k,k-1}y_{k-1}=0\), so \(y_{k-1}=0\). Continue upwards to obtain all entries zero. Thus the reduced matrix has full column rank and its least-squares minimizer is unique. This is the standard GMRES reduction (Saad and Schultz 1986; Saad 2003).

WarningExercise

Before Arnoldi breakdown, show that \(\bar{\bH}_k\) has full column rank. Start with its last row and use the nonzero subdiagonal entries to show that \(\bar{\bH}_k\by=\bzero\) implies \(\by=\bzero\). Then use least-squares orthogonality to prove \(\br^{(k)}\perp\bA\mathcal K_k\). Explain why enlarging the subspace cannot increase the minimum residual norm.

NoteTheorem: Polynomial Residual Characterization and Spectral Bound

The \(k\)-th GMRES residual satisfies the polynomial minimization property \[ \begin{align} \|\br^{(k)}\|_2 = \min_{p \in \mathcal{P}_k,\, p(0)=1} \|p(\bA)\br^{(0)}\|_2. \end{align} \] If \(\bA\) is diagonalizable with \(\bA = \bX \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \bX^{-1}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_n)\), then the relative residual is bounded by \[ \begin{align} \frac{\|\br^{(k)}\|_2}{\|\br^{(0)}\|_2} \leq \kappa_2(\bX) \min_{p \in \mathcal{P}_k,\, p(0)=1} \max_{\lambda \in \sigma(\bA)} |p(\lambda)|. \end{align} \]

TipProof

Write a general Krylov correction using its generating powers: \[ \begin{align} \bx-\bx^{(0)}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j\bA^j\br^{(0)} =q(\bA)\br^{(0)},\qquad q(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_jt^j. \end{align} \] Multiplication by \(\bA\) and subtraction from the initial residual gives \[ \begin{align} \br(\bx)&=\br^{(0)}-\bA q(\bA)\br^{(0)}\\ &=[\bI-\bA q(\bA)]\br^{(0)}=p(\bA)\br^{(0)}, \end{align} \] where \(p(t)=1-tq(t)\) has degree at most \(k\) and satisfies \(p(0)=1\).

Conversely, let \(p(t)=1+a_1t+\cdots+a_kt^k\). Then \(q(t)=-a_1-a_2t-\cdots-a_kt^{k-1}\) is a polynomial and \(p(t)=1-tq(t)\). Thus every normalized polynomial in the statement corresponds to an admissible correction. GMRES minimizes over exactly this set, proving the first equality.

Now assume diagonalizability, \(\bA=\bX\boldsymbol\Lambda\bX^{-1}\). Induction gives \(\bA^j=\bX\boldsymbol\Lambda^j\bX^{-1}\), and substituting these powers into a polynomial gives \(p(\bA)=\bX p(\boldsymbol\Lambda)\bX^{-1}\). For any admissible \(p\), \[ \begin{align} \|p(\bA)\br^{(0)}\|_2 &\leq\|\bX\|_2\|p(\boldsymbol\Lambda)\|_2 \|\bX^{-1}\|_2\|\br^{(0)}\|_2\\ &=\kappa_2(\bX)\max_i|p(\lambda_i)|\|\br^{(0)}\|_2. \end{align} \] The Euclidean norm of a diagonal matrix is its largest diagonal magnitude, which explains the last equality. GMRES has residual no larger than that of this particular candidate. Taking the minimum of the upper bound over admissible polynomials and dividing by the nonzero initial residual norm proves the spectral estimate. If the initial residual is zero, the system is already solved and no relative ratio is needed.

26.2 Givens Rotations

NoteTheorem: Incremental QR Factorization of the Hessenberg Matrix

At step \(k\), applying the previously accumulated Givens rotations \(\bG_1, ..., \bG_{k-1}\) transforms the first \(k-1\) entries of the new column of \(\bar{\bH}_k\). The subdiagonal entry at position \((k+1, k)\) is then eliminated using a new Givens rotation \(\bG_k\) defined by \[ \begin{align} \bG_k = \begin{pmatrix} c_k & s_k \\ -s_k & c_k \end{pmatrix}, \qquad c_k = \frac{h_{kk}^{(k-1)}}{\sqrt{(h_{kk}^{(k-1)})^2 + h_{k+1,k}^2}}, \quad s_k = \frac{h_{k+1,k}}{\sqrt{(h_{kk}^{(k-1)})^2 + h_{k+1,k}^2}}. \end{align} \] Applying \(\bG_k ... \bG_1\) transforms \(\bar{\bH}_k\) into an upper triangular matrix \(\bR_k\) with a zero final row, and transforms the right-hand side vector \(\beta \be_1\) into \(\bg_{k+1} = (\gamma_1, ..., \gamma_k, \gamma_{k+1})^T\). The residual norm at iteration \(k\) is obtained without forming \(\bx^{(k)}\): \[ \begin{align} \|\br^{(k)}\|_2 = |\gamma_{k+1}|. \end{align} \]

TipProof

Each plane rotation acts as an orthogonal matrix on the full \((k+1)\)-dimensional space by leaving the other coordinates unchanged. Their product \(\bQ_k=\bG_k\cdots\bG_1\) is therefore orthogonal and preserves Euclidean norms.

The first \(k-1\) rotations are already known from the preceding step. Applying them to the new column leaves only one possible subdiagonal entry. The new rotation removes it. Thus \[ \begin{align} \bQ_k\bar{\bH}_k=\begin{pmatrix}\bR_k\\\bzero^T\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \bQ_k(\beta\be_1)=\begin{pmatrix}\bg_{1:k}\\\gamma_{k+1}\end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \] Here \(\bR_k\) is \(k\times k\). It is nonsingular because rotations preserve rank and \(\bar{\bH}_k\) has full column rank before breakdown.

For any coefficient vector \(\by\), preserve the norm by applying \(\bQ_k\), then separate the last coordinate: \[ \begin{align} \|\beta\be_1-\bar{\bH}_k\by\|_2^2 &=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}\bg_{1:k}-\bR_k\by\\\gamma_{k+1}\end{pmatrix}\right\|_2^2\\ &=\|\bg_{1:k}-\bR_k\by\|_2^2+|\gamma_{k+1}|^2. \end{align} \] The last summand does not depend on \(\by\), so it is a lower bound for the squared residual. Solve the triangular system \(\bR_k\by=\bg_{1:k}\) to make the first summand zero. Hence that lower bound is attained, and the minimum residual norm is exactly \(|\gamma_{k+1}|\).

Only the transformed right-hand side is needed to read this norm. Forming the full iterate \(\bx^{(0)}+\bV_k\by\) can wait until the stopping test is satisfied.

TipRemark

(Happy breakdown vs. stagnation) If the subdiagonal entry \(h_{k+1,k}\) vanishes, the referenced result shows that the Krylov subspace is invariant under \(\bA\). When \(\bA\) is nonsingular, its restriction to this invariant subspace is nonsingular, so the GMRES least-squares problem has residual zero and \(\bx^{(k)}\) is the exact solution. Termination for this reason is called happy breakdown. Stagnation is a different phenomenon. The Krylov space may continue to grow while its image under \(\bA\) contributes no useful correction to the residual. Non-normality, an unfavorable polynomial approximation problem, or a poor preconditioner can all cause this behavior, and the residual history alone does not identify which one is responsible.

26.3 Restarted GMRES and Practical Considerations

NoteDefinition: Restarted GMRES(\(m\))

Full GMRES requires storing \(k\) basis vectors of length \(n\), incurring \(O(kn)\) memory storage and \(O(k^2 n)\) orthogonalization flops. To avoid memory exhaustion on large systems, the algorithm is restarted every \(m\) steps:

  1. Run \(m\) steps of GMRES starting from \(\bx^{(0)}\) to produce \(\bx^{(m)}\).

  2. Compute the residual \(\br^{(m)} = \bb - \bA\bx^{(m)}\).

  3. Clear the Krylov basis vectors, set \(\bx^{(0)} \leftarrow \bx^{(m)}\), and repeat.

WarningExercise

(Left versus right preconditioning) Compare left preconditioning (\(\bM^{-1}\bA\bx = \bM^{-1}\bb\)) and right preconditioning (\(\bA\bM^{-1}\by = \bb\), \(\bx = \bM^{-1}\by\)). Show that right-preconditioned GMRES minimizes the true residual \(\|\bb-\bA\bx\|_2\), whereas left-preconditioned GMRES minimizes \(\|\bM^{-1}(\bb-\bA\bx)\|_2\). Explain why a code that uses left preconditioning may need to monitor both quantities.

TipRemark

(The trade-off of restarting) Restarted GMRES(\(m\)) bounds memory usage to \(O(mn)\) and bounds orthogonalization cost per cycle. However, restarting discards the accumulated Krylov subspace and destroys the global optimality property. If \(m\) is chosen too small, the algorithm may stagnate completely.

26.4 Further Exercises

WarningExercise

(Arnoldi factorization by hand) For the matrix and initial residual \[ \begin{align} \bA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \br^{(0)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \end{align} \] perform two steps of the Arnoldi iteration by hand.

  1. Compute \(\bv_1\) and \(\bw_1 = \bA\bv_1\). Find \(h_{11}, h_{21}\) and \(\bv_2\).

  2. Compute \(\bw_2 = \bA\bv_2\). Find \(h_{12}, h_{22}, h_{32}\) and \(\bv_3\).

  3. Explicitly assemble the matrices \(\bV_2\) and the \(3 \times 2\) upper Hessenberg matrix \(\bar{\bH}_2\).

WarningExercise

(Hessenberg QR and residual norm via Givens) Using the \(3 \times 2\) matrix \(\bar{\bH}_2\) from the preceding Arnoldi exercise:

  1. Form the Givens rotation \(\bG_1\) that eliminates \(h_{21}\), and the rotation \(\bG_2\) that eliminates \(h_{32}\).

  2. Apply these rotations to the right-hand side vector \(\beta \be_1 = (\sqrt{2}, 0, 0)^T\).

  3. Read off the residual norm \(\|\br^{(2)}\|_2\) from the transformed vector without computing \(\bx^{(2)}\).

WarningExercise

(GMRES polynomial minimax on an ellipse) Suppose the eigenvalues of \(\bA\) are enclosed within an ellipse in the complex plane centered at \(c > 0\) with focal distance \(d < c\) that does not contain the origin.

  1. Using the scaled Chebyshev polynomial \(p(z) = T_k((c - z)/d) / T_k(c/d)\), show that \(p(0) = 1\).

  2. Apply the referenced result to derive an explicit upper bound for \(\|\br^{(k)}\|_2 / \|\br^{(0)}\|_2\) in terms of the semi-axes of the ellipse.

WarningExercise

(Exact stagnation for a cyclic permutation) Let \(\bA\) be the cyclic permutation matrix defined by \(\bA\be_j=\be_{j+1}\) for \(j<n\) and \(\bA\be_n=\be_1\). Take \(\bx^{(0)}=\bzero\) and \(\bb=\be_1\).

  1. Prove that \(\mathcal{K}_k(\bA,\bb)=\operatorname{span}\{\be_1,...,\be_k\}\) for \(k<n\).

  2. Show that \(\bA\mathcal{K}_k=\operatorname{span}\{\be_2,...,\be_{k+1}\}\) is orthogonal to \(\bb\). Conclude that \(\|\br^{(k)}\|_2=1\) for every \(k<n\).

  3. Show that \(\bx=\be_n\) becomes available at step \(n\) and gives zero residual. Construct the degree-\(n\) residual polynomial that vanishes on the spectrum of \(\bA\), and explain why no polynomial of smaller degree can do so.
